description: KiyoSpace is a multidisciplinary team of passionate engineers and innovators dedicated to advancing space exploration. By combining physics, artificial intelligence, and engineering, we aim to transform NASA's data into practical solutions for safer and smarter lunar missions.
summary:
KiyoSPACE is an AI-assisted lunar mission planning and replanning platform developed for NASA's Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. It aims to transform complex lunar terrain and astronomical data into accessible, actionable mission decisions.

Using NASA lunar topography, JPL SPICE ephemerides, and machine learning, KiyoSPACE is designed to compare landing sites and dates, predict solar illumination and Earth visibility, and evaluate energy availability and mission constraints.

Our key innovation addresses **“Phantom Mission Windows”**—situations where a landing opportunity appears favorable based on visibility but may not support scientific operations or timely data delivery.

Beyond traditional landing-site assessment, KiyoSPACE explores physics-constrained mission recovery when schedules change, helping identify alternative sites, dates, and operational strategies.

By combining scientific modeling, explainable AI, and interactive visualization, KiyoSPACE aims to improve mission-planning efficiency, scientific accessibility, and sustainable lunar exploration.
details:
KiyoSPACE — Beyond Landing Windows, Toward Mission Success

1. The Problem: When Visibility Does Not Guarantee Mission Success

Planning a mission to the lunar south pole involves more than selecting an illuminated landing site. The region's extreme terrain, rapidly changing shadows, limited solar-energy opportunities, and intermittent direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication create interconnected operational constraints.

Existing NASA resources provide valuable lunar terrain and astronomical information, but comparing multiple sites, dates, and mission-specific requirements can require complex analysis.

KiyoSPACE investigates a critical planning challenge we call “Phantom Mission Windows”: situations where Sun and Earth visibility appear favorable, yet a mission may lack sufficient energy, operational time, or communication capacity to complete its scientific objectives.

Our central question is:

Can a lunar lander complete its scientific mission under changing environmental and scheduling constraints—and how can its operations be recovered when the original plan becomes infeasible?

2. Our Solution: KiyoSPACE

KiyoSPACE is an interactive lunar mission intelligence platform designed to connect geospatial analysis, physics-based simulation, machine learning, and mission-replanning optimization.

Our dashboard allows users to select and compare lunar landing locations, mission start dates, simulation durations, solar-panel configurations, battery capacities, and electrical loads.

The system is designed around four interconnected capabilities:

A. Lunar Landing Site Intelligence

NASA LOLA digital elevation models provide topographic information. An experimental LightGBM-based spatial predictor supports candidate-site assessment, while computer vision architectures such as ResNet-50 and NASA–IBM's Lunar Foundation Model are considered for more advanced terrain analysis.

Geographic coordinates must be derived from valid lunar geospatial information rather than generated by AI alone.

B. Physics-Based Environmental Prediction

JPL SPICE provides astronomical geometry for the Sun and Earth. Terrain-aware calculations are designed to evaluate illumination, solar-power opportunities, and direct-to-Earth line-of-sight.

A time-dependent energy model estimates photovoltaic generation, electrical consumption, and battery state of charge under different mission scenarios.

C. Mission Deliverability Assessment

KiyoSPACE extends beyond visibility analysis by considering how scientific activities, battery availability, onboard data storage, and communication opportunities interact over time.

This enables evaluation of whether a selected landing opportunity can meet mission-specific operational requirements.

D. Mission Recovery Intelligence

When a landing date changes, the proposed recovery framework compares the original scenario with delayed or alternative missions.

Constraint-based optimization, including CP-SAT or mixed-integer programming, is intended to identify operational schedules that satisfy energy, communication, storage, and scientific deadlines.

3. What Makes KiyoSPACE Different?

Traditional visibility screening asks: “When can the Sun and Earth be seen?”

KiyoSPACE asks: “Can the mission actually deliver its scientific objectives, and what can be changed if it cannot?”

Its proposed innovation combines:

  • Predict: Evaluate lunar illumination, energy availability, and communication opportunities.
  • Detect: Identify mission windows that fail operational constraints despite favorable visibility.
  • Recover: Explore alternative landing dates, locations, and activity schedules.
  • Verify: Check candidate solutions against explicit physical and operational constraints.

KiyoSPACE prioritizes explainable, physics-grounded decisions over unsupported black-box predictions.

4. Technologies and Development Tools

The technical architecture uses or proposes the following components:

  • NASA Data: Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA), Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery, and lunar topography products.
  • Astronomical Modeling: NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE.
  • Programming: Python for simulation, numerical analysis, and machine-learning integration.
  • Machine Learning: LightGBM for experimental spatial site prediction; ResNet-50 and lunar foundation models as candidates for terrain-analysis development.
  • Backend: FastAPI for connecting the interface with prediction and simulation services.
  • Numerical Methods: Terrain-horizon analysis, temporal energy simulation, numerical integration, and constraint verification.
  • Optimization: Proposed OR-Tools CP-SAT or MILP for mission recovery.
  • Visualization: Interactive web dashboard with lunar site selection, scenario parameters, and comparative mission indicators.

The architecture separates machine-learning predictions from deterministic physical calculations to preserve transparency and reproducibility.

5. Technical Validation and Development Status

The project includes an interactive dashboard prototype and an architecture for comparing lunar mission scenarios.

Illustrative simulations have been used to examine situations where equal visibility percentages produce different scientific-data delivery outcomes due to the timing of communication windows.

These tests demonstrate the underlying modeling principle but do not constitute flight validation or independent verification against real lunar mission operations.

Full backend integration, lunar-data validation, predictive-model benchmarking, and automated mission-recovery optimization remain development and verification objectives.

Planned validation includes comparisons with JPL reference ephemerides, numerical convergence testing, energy-balance checks, and evaluation against baseline mission-screening methods.

6. Scientific, Economic, Social, and Environmental Impact

Scientific Impact: Support clearer evaluation of landing opportunities and potential scientific-data delivery under mission constraints.

Economic Impact: Reduce repetitive preliminary mission-analysis work and improve the efficiency of engineering trade studies. An illustrative techno-economic model has been developed, but projected cost savings remain assumptions pending user validation.

Social Impact: Make complex lunar mission analysis more accessible to students, educators, researchers, and emerging space-technology communities.

Environmental Impact: Encourage resource-efficient lunar operations and support future integration of scientifically sensitive lunar-region screening, including permanently shadowed regions.

7. Our Vision

KiyoSPACE aims to evolve from an interactive lunar mission navigator into a transparent, physics-grounded platform for operational decision support.

By connecting NASA's scientific data with AI-assisted analysis and mission recovery, we seek to make future lunar exploration more resilient, efficient, accessible, and scientifically productive.

KiyoSPACE — Landing Is Just the Beginning. Deliver the Discovery.
